newsitem.title: HUNGARY: GROWING HUNGARIAN BUSMAKER NABI TURNS TO AIR CARGO.
newsitem.headline: GROWING HUNGARIAN BUSMAKER NABI TURNS TO AIR CARGO.

text.p: Hungary's North American Bus Industries Rt (NABI), the only east European automaker to build and sell vehicles in the United States, has started using air cargo regularly to support a boom in its sales.
"When our business started four years ago, we used air cargo irregularly, but we have multiplied our output, and our transport needs have grown," NABI's sales director Katalin Patkos told Reuters.
"Now we ship 600 to 800 kilograms a week by air, and freight forwarders are knocking on our door almost every day for this business," Patkos added.

NABI, which last month announced plans to list some of its shares on the Budapest Stock Exchange, relies on a range of transport to keep on schedule a complex production system that crosses the Atlantic Ocean twice each time a bus is completed.

The company, now wholly owned by the First Hungary Fund of the Jersey Channel Islands, installs U.S.-built axles in Budapest on Hungarian-made bus bodies and chassis. These shells are sent to the United States for final assembly with U.S-built engines, transmissions and wheelchair lifts, she said.

The axles normally arrive in Budapest by sea, while the shells travel to America on low-bed rail cars to Bremerhaven, Germany, continuing by sea to Charleston, South Carolina and arriving by truck at the assembly plant in Anniston, Alabama, Patkos said.
But air cargo has become essential to avoid production delays in managing inventory and replacement parts, she said.

"It may be possible to build 10,000 identical passenger cars, but there are big differences in customer requirements and technical specifications for even small orders of buses," Patkos said, noting that an order for a single bus can fill hundreds of pages.

"Design changes and last-minute customer requests make it impossible for us always to have the right parts at the right time," she added. "And there are ever-shorter periods for us to engineer, test and deliver a finished bus. This challenges the limits of our schedule as well as our suppliers."

NABI's air cargo mainly comprises compact-and-heavy parts made of material like fiberglass, metal and rubber, Patkos said. Single consignments often are over 300 kilograms, which enable NABI to command low rates, she added.
"It's more expensive to ship feathers," she said.

NABI sends its air cargo to Atlanta, the major international airport closest to its Alabama plant, but it still sees rates for large shipments near the bargain prices of $1.00-$1.30 per kilo for deliveries from Budapest to New York.
Since NABI started using air cargo on roughly a weekly basis, the costs for its shipments also have dropped sharply, she said.

"We paid almost double per kilo two years ago because our shipments were irregular," Patkos said. "The regularity and volume of our shipments has brought down the rates. I hope that rates will continue to decrease, but I don't expect anything dramatic."
NABI's air cargo use has followed a big jump in business, as bus production has soared from 49 units in 1994 to 292 units in 1996, Patkos said.
And NABI -- specialising in 40-and-60-foot-long heavy-duty buses for U.S. city and county transit services -- expects its output to surpass 400 units in 1997, she said.

Buses already have been sold to Baltimore, Maryland; Buffalo, New York; Miami; Oakland, California; Philadelphia; and Washington, DC. NABI also has orders from Las Vegas as well as Phoenix and Tempe, Arizona.
"At the top of our capacity, we could build 500-550 buses of this type a year," Patkos said.

"We also are studying another segment of the U.S. bus market to enter -- the demand for 25-foot-long to 30-foot-long buses for customers like car rental agents, tourist businesses and other public and private operators."

NABI, which recently launched plans for a capital increase and an initial public offering of shares, on Tuesday fixed the subscription price of a global equity offering at 3,280 forints per share, effectively valuing the company at 14.7 billion forints.
